characters: Dari: a lively seven-year-old Ghanaian schoolgirl with neat braided plaits, wearing a sky-blue-and-navy school uniform dress.
Akuffo: her cheerful seven-year-old Ghanaian classmate with short hair, wearing a sky-blue collared shirt and navy school shorts.
Madam Kumi: their warm Ghanaian class teacher wearing a bright emerald-and-gold African-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: A lively girl’s voice for Dari; a cheerful boy’s voice for Akuffo; a kind, clear teacher voice for Madam Kumi
narrationPlan.pace: Clear and steady, with a count for the scrub (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light, splashy tune with a counting beat (placeholder)
culturalNotes: A Veronica bucket—invented in Ghana by biological scientist Veronica Bekoe—is a covered bucket with a tap near the bottom set on a stand over a catch-bowl so people can wash their hands under clean running water.
The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on personal hygiene (B1.5.1.1, B2.5.1.1) and on keeping the school and compound clean (B2.5.1.1.2).
Handwashing steps: wet, soap, scrub (about 20 seconds), rinse, dry. The story suggests singing a short song twice as a timer. Teachers should confirm with Ghana Health Service guidance.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check the handwashing steps and the times (before eating, after using the toilet, after playing outside, after coughing or sneezing into the hands, after touching animals) against Ghana Health Service guidance.
Check that the bucket and the tap are used safely and that the wastewater is not left standing where mosquitoes could breed.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about washing hands properly with soap at a Veronica bucket. It teaches why soap matters, the steps and the times for handwashing, and keeping the area clean. Based on the NaCCA Science standards on personal hygiene.
learningGoals: Say why we wash hands with soap.
Say the five handwashing steps in order.
Name four times when we wash our hands.
beforeReading: Ask: when do you wash your hands? How do you do it?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 and have children mime each step.
afterReading: Set up a Veronica bucket or a tap, soap and a bowl, and practise the steps with a teacher watching.
Make a poster of the five steps and four times.
discussion: Why is water alone not enough?
Why do we pour the bowl water into a drain?
reflection: When will you wash your hands tonight?

support: Use five picture cards for the steps and put them in order.
stretch: Count how many times your class washes hands in one school day.

culturalNotes: A Veronica bucket—invented in Ghana by biological scientist Veronica Bekoe—is a covered bucket with a tap near the bottom set on a stand over a catch-bowl so people can wash their hands under clean running water.
The story follows the NaCCA Science standards on personal hygiene (B1.5.1.1, B2.5.1.1) and on keeping the school and compound clean (B2.5.1.1.2).
Handwashing steps: wet, soap, scrub (about 20 seconds), rinse, dry. The story suggests singing a short song twice as a timer. Teachers should confirm with Ghana Health Service guidance.
localiseThis: Use the water source, soap and hand-washing points that your school really has.
Do not let used water stand in puddles; pour it into a drain or onto plants.

factCheck.explanation: Confirm the handwashing steps and times with Ghana Health Service guidance and NaCCA B1.5.1.1 and B2.5.1.1.
